---
title: "College Majors, AI Exposure, and Pay"
format: html
---

## Question

Among the majors with the lowest AI exposure, which ones have the highest starting salaries?

## Data

The data come from the [TidyTuesday project](https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/tree/main/data/2026/2026-10-20).
They combine starting salaries from the College Scorecard with estimates of occupational exposure to AI.
A lower AI exposure percentile means that the major is less exposed relative to other majors in this dataset.

```{r}
#| message: false

library(tidyverse)

majors <- read_csv(
  "ai_salary_majors.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
```

## Visualization

```{r}
safe_majors <- majors %>%
  filter(ai_exposure_percentile <= 20) %>%
  slice_max(median_starting_salary, n = 10) %>%
  mutate(major = str_wrap(field_of_study, width = 30))

ggplot(
  safe_majors,
  aes(
    x = median_starting_salary,
    y = reorder(major, median_starting_salary)
  )
) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(
    title = "Low AI exposure can still come with high pay",
    subtitle = "Ten highest-paid majors among the lowest 20% in AI exposure",
    x = "Median starting salary",
    y = NULL,
    caption = "TidyTuesday 2026-10-20 | Sources: College Scorecard and AIOE"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

The majors shown here are all in the lowest 20% of AI exposure in the dataset, but their starting salaries still vary.
Several hands-on engineering and technical programs appear near the top.
AI exposure measures how much a job's tasks overlap with AI abilities, so low exposure does not guarantee that a job is completely safe from automation.
